title: India Objects to UN Map Depicting Arunachal, Aksai Chin as Separate Regions
excerpt: New Delhi has engaged UN authorities over a world map showing Arunachal Pradesh and Aksai Chin as separate regions, insisting its vote for the 'Correct the Map' resolution endorsed no border claims.
body:
• India has raised concerns with the United Nations over a new world map that depicts Arunachal Pradesh as a state independent of India and Aksai Chin as a region separate from both India and China.
  • The Ministry of External Affairs said it has engaged UN authorities to address the cartographic inaccuracies, calling them inconsistent with India's official map.
  • The friction follows India's vote in favor of the UN General Assembly's African Union-backed "Correct the Map" resolution on September 4 — a non-binding measure New Delhi says it backed only for equal-area map projections, not border claims.
  • The UN has not explained the depictions, which echo long-running Chinese territorial claims over both regions.

India has formally raised objections with the United Nations over a newly published world map that depicts Arunachal Pradesh as a state independent of India and Aksai Chin as a region separate from both Indian and Chinese control, prompting a swift diplomatic response from New Delhi.

The map, first published by the UN on July 1, removes Arunachal Pradesh's border with Nagaland and shows it as a separate entity bordering Assam and China. Aksai Chin is displayed as a distinct region with its western side bordering India and its eastern side bordering China. The UN has not explained the changes.

India's response

The Ministry of External Affairs confirmed it has already engaged with relevant UN authorities to address the inaccuracies. New Delhi has consistently held that Arunachal Pradesh and the Union Territory of Ladakh — which includes Aksai Chin — are integral and inalienable parts of its sovereign territory.

At his weekly media briefing, MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal drew a firm line between the controversy and India's vote for the African Union-backed "Correct the Map" resolution, adopted by the UN General Assembly on September 4. The resolution, which is non-binding, encourages member states and international bodies to use equal-area projections that represent countries' relative sizes more accurately, and is expected to influence standard maps used by multilateral institutions.

"The resolution neither adopts nor authenticates any particular world map, nor does it address political cartography, including international boundaries, disputed territories or place names."

— Randhir Jaiswal, Spokesperson, Ministry of External Affairs

The ministry said India's vote supported the principle of equal-area cartographic representation and did not amount to endorsing any specific map, projection or depiction of national boundaries.

A dispute with deep history

The cartographic friction lands on a long-standing territorial dispute. China claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of "southern Tibet" and in April 2023 renamed 11 places in the state. Beijing's August 2023 release of an official "standard map" claiming both regions prompted a strong diplomatic protest from New Delhi. Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar said at the time that "making absurd claims on India's territory does not make it China's territory."

Aksai Chin, a high-altitude plateau in the western Himalayas claimed by India but controlled by China, was the flashpoint of the June 2020 Galwan Valley clash that killed 20 Indian soldiers and four Chinese troops. Relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbours have remained strained since.

The map's other contentious detail

The UN map also uses a dotted line to mark the Line of Control dividing Jammu and Kashmir between India and Pakistan, with a footnote stating that the line represents approximately the LoC agreed upon by the two countries and that "the final status of Jammu and Kashmir has not been agreed upon by the parties." India has not accepted that framing either: Jaiswal said the country's sovereign territory, including the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, "must be depicted in accordance with India's official map."

"Any inaccurate or misleading depiction is unacceptable. Our position on India's sovereignty and territorial integrity is clear, consistent and non-negotiable."

— Randhir Jaiswal, Spokesperson, Ministry of External Affairs

What it means for the diaspora

For Indians abroad, UN cartography matters more than it might seem: multilateral institutions' standard maps flow into textbooks, digital platforms and news graphics worldwide, quietly shaping how the next generation sees India's borders. New Delhi's insistence that a technical resolution on map projections cannot be repurposed as a verdict on political boundaries is aimed at exactly that downstream influence. The episode also mirrors a broader pattern the diaspora has watched before — official Chinese maps have repeatedly triggered protests from New Delhi, and each incident tends to reverberate in Indian communities globally.

What to watch

India has not said whether the UN has responded to its outreach, and the world body has offered no public explanation. Watch for any correction from UN cartographic authorities — and for whether the "Correct the Map" resolution's push for new standard maps produces further depictions India deems inaccurate. New Delhi's warning that supporting the resolution was not an endorsement of any map leaves little room for ambiguity about how it will react if more appear.
nri_angle: Standard UN maps shape textbooks and digital platforms worldwide, so India's challenge aims to stop an inaccurate depiction of its borders from becoming the default the next generation sees.
